lesson_title: The Comma That Walks: Scientific Notation
hook_text: Earth to Sun: 149 600 000 km. A red blood cell: 0,0000075 m. Same trick writes both in five characters.
clip_script: Scientific notation is a decimal comma taking a walk. Take 149 600 000. The comma wants to sit after the first digit: 1,496. How far did it walk? Eight jumps. So it is 1,496 times 10 to the power 8 — the 8 remembers the walk. Now a tiny number: 0,0000075. The comma walks the other way, six jumps right, to make 7,5. Walking right means the exponent is negative: 7,5 times 10 to the power negative 6. And here is the trap: that minus is a direction for the comma, not a sign on the number. 10 to the power negative 4 is 0,0001 — small, but positive. One digit in front of the comma, count the jumps, done.
visual_style: A long number on a whiteboard; a glowing comma hops left one digit at a time with a counter ticking to 8, then a tiny decimal with the comma hopping right to 6, the exponent flipping to negative in red.
pacing: Brisk hops with a deliberate pause on the negative-exponent trap.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any number the universe throws at you.
